item.title: The Disappearers
item.description: After my eyes were molested by the pretentious filth in Life of M and I was in desperate need of a palette cleanser, The Disappearers was published. It’s by a real Writer named Marlon James and it lives up to the hype and more! It was nice to leave behind the pretentiousness of Rachel Cusk’s autofiction, a style which feels like a gentrification of life experiences. I was happy to return to the dark and depraved world of Marlon James’ Jamaica.

item.title: Life of M: Sense of Self and What Even Is A Character?
item.description: Two and a half years ago I moved out of my home country, from San Francisco to Berlin. I was twenty six years old two and a half years ago. In leaving a cosmopolitan lifestyle on the West Coast in the U.S. to experience what ultimately became an almost identical cosmopolitan experience in a new country, I had convinced myself that by making a move like this I was achieving a Sense of Self! It’s ridiculous, of course!

item.title: Been Down So Long It Looks Like Up To Me
item.description:
Been Down So Long it Looks Like Up to Me, by Richard Farina

Gnossos Pappadapoulis’ central conflict is that he is desperately in search of something sincere and real, but reality has been so shitty and terrified him to the point of retreating into hedonism; he uses drugs and postures a detached coolness as a means by which he can extract himself from a grim and confusing reality. There’s a lot about this vague search for meaning through exemption while also pushing back against conservatism, somewhat. Hedonism as a sort of vague form of protest: where have we seen this before?

item.title: Kairos, Age Gap Relationships and Bad Weather
item.description: I’d love to skip this one. Book sucked in my opinion. Jenny Erpenbeck has got a fucked up sense of humor because why was the ideal vessel for exploring post-reunification life in Berlin a relationship between a man who is something like fifty-four and a nineteen year old girl? I understand that their relationship is a metaphor for having completely different understandings and feelings of nostalgia for the East Germany you grew up in; a sixty year old man and a teenage girl would definitely experience newly reunified Berlin differently if they both experienced coming-of-age in East Berlin but during completely different times of their lives.

item.title: Vineland
item.description:
1. Vineland, by Thomas Pynchon

    Like any other Pynchon book, especially reading for the first time, you’re supposed to let yourself get lost, though this is apparently one of his most accessible works, or maybe even Pynchon-lite. Nevertheless I might not even be keen enough to get a grip on Pynchon-lite as I was still almost completely lost.

    Though it was published in 1990 it’s still extremely prescient, clearly. It’s very broadly about the free spirits of the 60s helplessly watching America march forward into the 80s as if in the blink of an eye, and contending with the fact that their project failed. What is it about this cultural moment? Why do we hear more from the people of 60s counterculture than seemingly any American generation? It’s probably one of the most run-through tropes, these geezers who smoked pot, went to Woodstock, and protested the Vietnam War… they lost; and we will never hear the end of it. It’s as if they kind of gave it their all in trying out this Great Society experiment and never got over the trauma of seeing the fascistic repression of the Nixon years play out. This is also a book that is very broadly about a repressive police state. I think it goes without saying that the police state we live in, even before the last two years, probably outdoes Pynchon’s worst imaginations when writing Brock Vond and his goons in Vineland.

    It’s clear that there’s a consensus feeling that the rightward backlash of the Nixon years were some sort of revenge against the hippies? Certainly this is what both Trump presidencies have felt like for us. But what was our Woodstock? I don’t even remember the years before 2016 even being very cool or transgressive. What are they even so angry about?
